screens.title: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities and Exploits
screens.subtitle: Why a single flawed line of code can drain millions — and how to spot it

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on the most frequently exploited surface in blockchain systems: smart contract code that controls value and cannot be changed once deployed. You will learn to recognize the common classes of vulnerabilities that attackers repeatedly use: reentrancy that lets an external contract call back before state updates, integer overflow and underflow that can warp balances in older Solidity versions, weak access control that lets anyone assume privileged roles, front-running that abuses mempool visibility and transaction ordering, and denial-of-service vectors that make functions unusable by exhausting gas. Each of those problems has a clear mechanism and an equally clear pattern of code to watch for. We will examine canonical examples drawn from simple Solidity snippets, practice reasoning about real staking contract code, and discuss practical mitigations or design patterns that reduce risk. By the end of the lesson you will be able to read a short Solidity function and point to likely weaknesses, explain how an attacker could exploit them, and suggest the right defensive principle. Think of this chapter as training your security instincts: a single check you add today can prevent catastrophic losses tomorrow.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Smart contracts are immutable value controllers; small code errors map directly to financial loss. Identifying patterns is the first step to remediation.

screens.title: Reentrancy — how callback ordering breaks contracts
screens.subtitle: What reentrancy is, why external calls are risky, and the classic exploit pattern

narration.text: Reentrancy happens when a contract makes an external call to an untrusted contract and that external contract calls back into the original contract before the original contract has finished updating its state. The dangerous pattern is an external transfer or call occurring before the contract decrements balances or records that the withdrawal occurred. A canonical withdrawal function checks a balance, performs an external transfer, then updates the stored balance. If the recipient is a malicious contract, it can call back into withdraw repeatedly during the external transfer, each time passing the original balance check because the state update hasn't happened yet. The result is repeated withdrawals until the contract is drained. A concrete example in the lesson code shows a withdraw function that sends funds and then subtracts from balances; a malicious fallback triggers re-entry. A common misconception is to assume transfer semantics are atomic and always safe; in reality, any external call can transfer control flow. The key defensive insight is to follow a checks-effects-interactions discipline: perform internal checks, update state, then make external calls. For older patterns, pull-over-push payments and limiting external calls reduce exposure. Ask yourself when reading code: does any external call happen before every relevant state change? If so, reentrancy risk exists.

keyIdea.title: Reentrancy risk
keyIdea.text: External calls before state updates let an attacker repeatedly re-enter a function and drain funds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Reentrancy
Definition
Reentrancy explained
A reentrancy vulnerability allows an external contract to call back into a function before the original call finishes updating state, enabling repeated execution.
  • Cause: external call occurs before all state updates.
  • Effect: repeated execution bypasses balance changes.
  • Misconception: transfer is always safe — it is not when control is transferred to untrusted code.
Analogy
Imagine an ATM that sends cash before updating your account balance. A clever user can repeatedly request cash before the balance shows the withdrawal.
Key Takeaway

Always update internal state before making external calls. If you must call out, minimize exposed state and consider pull patterns.

Code example (vulnerable pattern)
// Vulnerable withdraw pattern
function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
}
This shows the external call occurring before the balance is updated, the exact trigger for reentrancy.
Check your understanding
Can a malicious recipient call withdraw again during the external call? Yes — until balances[msg.sender] is decremented. The fix is to reorder operations.
Common mistake: believing require checks before the external call prevent re-entry if state isn't updated.

screens.title: Reentrancy exploit sequence
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step how a malicious contract drains funds

narration.text: Let's walk through an attacker sequence to make the mechanics concrete. First, the attacker deploys a malicious contract that has a fallback or receive function which calls back into the vulnerable contract's withdraw function when it receives Ether. Second, the attacker funds the vulnerable contract by staking or depositing a small amount so an initial balance check passes. Third, the attacker begins the withdrawal; the vulnerable contract performs the external call to the attacker's contract. Fourth, during that external call, the malicious contract's fallback re-enters withdraw, repeating the external transfer while the vulnerable contract's balance record is still unchanged. This repeats until the vulnerable contract's Ether balance is exhausted. The misconception to avoid is thinking that making many small checks or gas-limiting will always stop the attack; the root issue is ordering and control transfer. A practical defensive check is to ensure state changes happen before any external interaction and to minimize external calls, or to use pull payments. When you review code, itemize the sequence: who initiates, where control flows, and when state is updated. That step-by-step thinking quickly reveals reentrancy windows.

keyIdea.title: Exploit pattern
keyIdea.text: An attacker re-enters during an external call to cause repeated execution before the state reflects prior transfers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Exploit Sequence
Attack steps
1
Deploy malicious contract
Malicious contract contains fallback logic that calls withdraw on receipt of Ether.
2
Seed a balance
Attacker ensures balances[msg.sender] is sufficient for the initial withdrawal check to pass.
3
Initiate withdraw
Vulnerable contract makes an external call to msg.sender without updating balances first.
4
Re-enter and repeat
Malicious fallback calls withdraw again. Balance check still passes because state wasn't changed, so funds are drained.
Common mistake: relying on gas costs or limited loops to stop reentrancy. The correct fix is ordering of state changes.
Concrete example
A withdraw function that transfers Ether before decrementing the sender's balance allows a malicious recipient to re-enter. Over many iterations, the attacker drains the contract balance fully despite initial balance checks.
Key Takeaway

Trace control flow: identify any external call that can transfer control before all related state changes are committed.

screens.title: Integer overflow and underflow
screens.subtitle: How arithmetic wrap-around corrupts token economics

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow occur when an arithmetic operation exceeds the representable range of an unsigned integer type and wraps to an unexpected value. In older Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0, arithmetic did not revert on overflow or underflow and instead silently wrapped around. For example, adding a large mint amount to a near-maximum total supply might wrap the value to a small number, and subtracting more than a current balance could underflow to a very large number, effectively granting an attacker huge token balances. The practical consequence of these bugs is direct economic distortion: attackers can mint astronomical amounts or make balances appear enormous. A common misconception is that integer errors are only theoretical; in deployed token contracts they changed ownership distributions and allowed theft. Solidity 0.8.0 introduced automatic reverts on wrap-around, mitigating many cases, but legacy contracts and custom arithmetic libraries still require care. When auditing, look for unchecked arithmetic in mint, burn, and reward functions, and ask if SafeMath or compiler checks are present. When you see arithmetic that scales with user input, treat it as high risk until proven safe.

keyIdea.title: Wrap-around danger
keyIdea.text: Unchecked arithmetic can wrap values, creating unrealistic balances or zeroing totals in older compilers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Integer Overflow & Underflow
Unsigned integer wrap
When a calculation exceeds the maximum or minimum representable value, arithmetic can wrap, producing incorrect results that attackers can exploit.
Why it matters
  • Token minting and burning often use direct arithmetic. A wrap can give an attacker huge balances.
  • Reward calculations that multiply user input can overflow if inputs are not bounded.
  • Compiler versions matter: pre-0.8.0 silently wrapped; newer compilers revert on wrap-around.
Common-mistake

Assuming the compiler always prevents wrap-around. Always verify compiler version and look for unchecked math in critical functions.

Code snippets
// Vulnerable when using older Solidity
uint public totalSupply;
function mint(uint _amount) public {
    totalSupply += _amount; // may overflow in pre-0.8.0
}

function burn(uint _amount) public {
    require(totalSupply >= _amount, "Insufficient supply");
    totalSupply -= _amount; // may underflow in pre-0.8.0
}
If totalSupply is near max(uint) and _amount is large, the addition wraps to a small number. If totalSupply is zero and you subtract a positive number, it may wrap to max(uint).
Key Takeaway

Audit arithmetic in mint, burn and reward logic. Verify compiler behaviour and use explicit checks or safe math where appropriate.

screens.title: Access control vulnerabilities
screens.subtitle: When missing checks let anyone change critical state

narration.text: Access control flaws occur when functions that should be restricted to an owner or a role are callable by anyone. In Solidity this commonly appears as a missing require that checks msg. sender against an owner address or missing role modifiers. The consequence is that an attacker can assume privileged actions: change configuration, transfer ownership, pause features, or drain funds. A simple example is a setOwner function that assigns a new owner without checking the caller. If an attacker calls that function they become owner and can then execute privileged functions. The misconception here is believing that only large code bases have such bugs; in practice a single missing check is sufficient. When auditing, list functions that modify critical state and verify they enforce correct checks or use a role-based access control library. Also consider initialization: constructors and ownership set-up must be airtight. Finally, threat model which addresses should have permission and what the impact of role compromise is. Clear, minimal, and auditable access checks prevent many high-severity exploits. Access control vulnerabilities means every state-changing function that affects funds or control must enforce the intended caller permissions.. In practical terms, when missing checks let anyone change critical state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access checks matter
keyIdea.text: Every state-changing function that affects funds or control must enforce the intended caller permissions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Access Control
Access control failures
Missing or incorrect checks allow any address to perform privileged actions intended for an owner or admin.
  • Look for functions that change contract configuration, pause, or transfer funds.
  • Check whether require(msg.sender == owner) or role checks exist; absence is a red flag.
  • Ensure constructor sets owner correctly and modifiers are applied consistently.
Common consequence

An attacker can change ownership or important parameters, often enabling theft or disabling protections.

Vulnerable pattern
// Vulnerable access control
address public owner;
function setOwner(address _newOwner) public {
    // Missing require(msg.sender == owner)
    owner = _newOwner;
}
Without a check on msg.sender, any external caller can set themselves as owner. That single missing line escalates privileges immediately.

screens.title: Front-running and the mempool
screens.subtitle: How transaction ordering can be abused and simple mitigations

narration.text: Front-running leverages the public visibility of pending transactions in the mempool. An attacker sees a profitable pending operation — for example, a large trade that will move a token price — and submits their own transaction with a higher gas price so miners include it first. This ordering advantage allows the attacker to profit at the victim's expense. While this is not a flaw in contract code itself, contracts that expose sensitive actions without protection can enable front-running. Examples include auction bids, atomic price-dependent trades, or any state mutation where ordering changes outcomes. Mitigations include commit-reveal schemes where a value is first committed and revealed later, batching transactions to reduce sensitivity to ordering, or redesigning logic to avoid price-sensitive single-step actions. A misconception is that front-running only happens on large networks; it occurs whenever pending transactions are visible. When reviewing a contract, identify functions where the observable input would let an attacker preemptively act, and consider commit, delay, or aggregation patterns to make ordering irrelevant. Front-running and the mempool means mempool visibility lets attackers reorder transactions for profit; protect order-sensitive flows with commit-reveal or batching.. In practical terms, how transaction ordering can be abused and simple mitigations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ordering risk
keyIdea.text: Mempool visibility lets attackers reorder transactions for profit; protect order-sensitive flows with commit-reveal or batching.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Front-running
Front-running via mempool
An attacker observes a pending transaction and submits a replacement with higher fees to get ahead. Contracts that depend on transaction order can be exploited this way.
Typical targets
  • Auctions and bidding contracts.
  • Decentralized exchanges and price-sensitive trades.
  • Any contract where visible inputs enable profitable ordering.
Mitigations
Use commit-reveal for sensitive inputs, batch operations to reduce granularity, or design logic that tolerates reordering. Remember that mempool visibility is a property of public blockchains.
Key Takeaway

Treat any function that can be economically influenced by transaction order as high risk and consider commit or batching patterns.

screens.title: Denial-of-Service via gas exhaustion
screens.subtitle: How unbounded loops or growth can make functions unusable

narration.text: Denial-of-service attacks aim to make a contract or its functions unusable. One common vector is gas exhaustion caused by unbounded loops over dynamic arrays or data structures that attackers can grow. If a function iterates over user-controlled lists and the list can be enlarged by any participant, an attacker can bloat the list until the function requires more gas than a block allows, preventing anyone from successfully calling it. For example, a processAllUsers function that loops over a userList without pagination can become unusable if an attacker keeps pushing addresses. The practical consequence is that critical maintenance functions may never run, locks may remain closed, or funds may become trapped. When auditing, look for loops over dynamic state and ask whether the list can be appended by untrusted users. Design alternatives include paginated processing, pull-based models where users finalize their own processing, or limiting who can add to the list. Misconception: thinking gas limits alone protect you; they determine the attack surface and cannot be relied upon as a security boundary. Denial-of-Service via gas exhaustion means unbounded iteration over attacker-controlled data enables gas exhaustion, blocking legitimate operations.. In practical terms, how unbounded loops or growth can make functions unusable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DoS by growth
keyIdea.text: Unbounded iteration over attacker-controlled data enables gas exhaustion, blocking legitimate operations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Denial-of-Service (DoS)
Gas-based DoS
Loops over dynamic data structures that can be grown by external users may eventually cost more gas than a block permits, making the function unusable.
  • Identify loops that iterate over arrays or maps without bounds.
  • Ask who can add items to those arrays; if anyone can, treat the loop as high risk.
  • Consider alternatives: pagination, batching, or pushing processing to users.
Vulnerable pattern
address[] public userList;
function addUser(address _user) public { userList.push(_user); }
function processAllUsers() public {
  for (uint i = 0; i < userList.length; i++) {
    // expensive work per user
  }
}
If one or more attackers append many addresses, processAllUsers will eventually require more gas than fits in a block, preventing its execution.
Key Takeaway

Avoid unbounded on-chain loops and design operations that can be performed incrementally or by the users themselves.

screens.title: Hands-on: StakingVulnerable.sol — withdraw() analysis
screens.subtitle: Identify the reentrancy window in the staking withdraw function

narration.text: We'll analyze the withdraw function from the provided StakingVulnerable contract to identify its vulnerabilities. The function requires the caller's staked balance to be at least the withdrawal amount, then makes an external call to msg. sender to send Ether, and only afterwards decrements the caller's stakedBalances and the totalStaked. That exact ordering creates a reentrancy window: during the external call, control moves to an untrusted contract that can call withdraw again, passing the initial balance check repeatedly while the stored balance is not yet reduced. An attacker with a malicious contract that receives Ether and immediately calls withdraw in its fallback can therefore drain the contract. A common mistake is assuming the require check alone prevents multiple withdrawals; it doesn't when state updates occur after the external transfer. When you report this vulnerability, point to the external call line and the subsequent state updates as the root cause, and note the exploit sequence: seed balance, call withdraw, re-enter via fallback, repeat until drained. As a reviewer, highlight the exact lines and recommend reordering updates before the transfer. Hands-on: StakingVulnerable.sol — withdraw() analysis means external call before state change enables reentrancy; reordering state updates prevents this specific exploit.. In practical terms, identify the reentrancy window in the staking withdraw function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Staking withdraw flaw
keyIdea.text: External call before state change enables reentrancy; reordering state updates prevents this specific exploit.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Staking: withdraw()
Vulnerable code excerpt
// withdraw(uint _amount)
require(stakedBalances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient staked balance");
(bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
stakedBalances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
totalStaked -= _amount;
This shows the external call to msg.sender before the state updates. A malicious recipient can use its fallback to re-enter withdraw during that call.
Key Takeaway

Flag the external call line and the delayed state updates; these two lines together define the reentrancy window.

Concrete attacker flow
  1. Deploy malicious contract with fallback that calls withdraw.
  2. Deposit a small amount so the balance check passes.
  3. Call withdraw; during the external transfer, fallback re-enters withdraw.
  4. Repeat until contract funds are exhausted.
Pro tip: When you annotate code, show the exact lines and explain the step where control transfers out of the contract.

screens.title: Hands-on: StakingVulnerable.sol — setOwner & getReward
screens.subtitle: Access control and arithmetic issues in the same contract

narration.text: The staking contract contains more than one issue. First, setOwner assigns owner without checking the caller, so anyone can call setOwner and become owner. The consequence is immediate privilege escalation: the attacker could later call owner-only functions or change critical parameters. When reporting this, note missing require or missing modifier that restricts access to owner. Second, getReward multiplies stakedBalances[msg. sender] by a supplied _multiplier to compute a reward. If _multiplier is unbounded and arithmetic is not checked, the multiplication can overflow in older compiler behaviour, producing astronomic reward values or unexpected wrap-around. In practice this could allow attackers to create very large rewards and drain token reserves or disrupt accounting. A useful audit comment will pair each vulnerability with a concrete exploit scenario: setOwner can be called to seize control, and getReward can be tricked by passing a huge multiplier to force wrap-around in pre-0.8.0 logic. Highlight both the function lines and the practical outcomes: privilege takeover and unrealistic reward creation. This combined analysis trains you to spot different classes of risks in one contract. Hands-on: StakingVulnerable.sol — setOwner & getReward means contracts frequently contain several independent vulnerabilities; report each separately with its concrete impact.. In practical terms, access control and arithmetic issues in the same contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multiple faults
keyIdea.text: Contracts frequently contain several independent vulnerabilities; report each separately with its concrete impact.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › setOwner & getReward
setOwner vulnerability
function setOwner(address _newOwner) public {
    // Missing require(msg.sender == owner)
    owner = _newOwner;
}
Consequence: Any caller can set a new owner and gain administrative capabilities. Record this as an immediate high-severity issue.
getReward arithmetic risk
uint reward = stakedBalances[msg.sender] * _multiplier;
If _multiplier is large and arithmetic is unchecked (older compiler), multiplication can overflow and produce an incorrect reward amount, enabling reward inflation or accounting errors.
Reporting guidance
  • List each vulnerable function, include exact line references, and describe the exploit scenario and impact.
  • For setOwner: suggest adding require(msg.sender == owner) or using a role-based access modifier.
  • For getReward: document the multiplication and note the need to bound inputs or use safe arithmetic depending on compiler guarantees.

screens.title: Mitigation patterns and misconceptions
screens.subtitle: Checks-Effects-Interactions, safe arithmetic, RBAC, and what they do (and don’t) guarantee

narration.text: When discussing mitigations, it's important to be precise about what each pattern prevents and what it leaves exposed. The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern rearranges code so internal checks and state updates happen before external calls. This directly prevents the classic reentrancy window because the attacker cannot re-enter and observe outdated state. Safe arithmetic — either using compiler versions that revert on wrap-around or using explicit checked libraries — prevents overflow and underflow in arithmetic operations. Role-based access control or explicit require checks prevent unauthorized callers from executing privileged functions. Commit-reveal and batching reduce front-running by decoupling visible inputs from immediate actions or by lowering sensitivity to ordering. However, no single pattern solves every problem: checks-effects-interactions won’t prevent front-running, and safe math won’t fix missing access checks. A common misconception is to apply a single mitigation everywhere; instead, match the pattern to the observed vulnerability class. When you write an audit recommendation, state which vulnerability you expect the mitigation to remove and which risks remain. Mitigation patterns and misconceptions means apply the right defensive pattern to the specific vulnerability class and be explicit about residual risks.. In practical terms, checks-effects-interactions, safe arithmetic, rbac, and what they do (and don’t) guarantee. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Targeted defenses
keyIdea.text: Apply the right defensive pattern to the specific vulnerability class and be explicit about residual risks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Mitigations
Checks-Effects-Interactions
Perform checks, update state, then do external interactions. This ordering closes the reentrancy window by ensuring state reflects the action before control leaves the contract.
Safe arithmetic
Use compiler versions that revert on overflow or explicit checked math. Audit multipliers and other user-controlled arithmetic inputs for bounds.
RBAC and require checks
Ensure functions that change sensitive state enforce identity checks through require or role modifiers. Confirm initialization sets owner correctly.
Order-sensitivity mitigations
Commit-reveal, batching, or delay reduce front-running exposure by hiding immediate intentions or grouping transactions.
Practical checklist for reviewers
  • Point to any external call and confirm state changed prior to that call.
  • Verify arithmetic on critical paths or require compiler-level checks.
  • List functions that modify control or money and confirm access checks exist and are consistent.
  • Flag loops over user-controlled arrays and suggest pagination or push patterns.

screens.title: Audit exercise: identify two vulnerabilities
screens.subtitle: Guided task using the staking contract as source material

narration.text: Now apply what you've learned in a short audit exercise. You are given the StakingVulnerable contract and asked to identify at least two distinct vulnerabilities. Approach the review systematically: first, scan each function for external calls and state updates. Mark any external call that happens before state mutation as a reentrancy candidate. Next, inspect functions that alter ownership or critical configuration and verify they include require checks that enforce intended callers. Then, review arithmetic operations that use user-supplied values, such as multipliers, and note whether arithmetic checks or safe compiler guarantees exist. For the provided contract, you'll find reentrancy in withdraw, access control absence in setOwner, and an arithmetic risk in getReward. When documenting findings, explain the exploit sequence, show a short attacker narrative, and describe the likely financial impact. Finally, prioritize your report: vulnerabilities that allow fund theft or privilege takeover get the highest severity. This methodical approach makes your audits clear and actionable. Audit exercise: identify two vulnerabilities means systematically check external calls, access checks, and arithmetic usage to identify exploitable patterns.. keyIdea.title: Audit method
keyIdea.text: Systematically check external calls, access checks, and arithmetic usage to identify exploitable patterns.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Audit Exercise
Guided steps
Step 1: Find external calls
List any call, transfer or callcode that hands control to another contract. Ask whether state has been updated first.
Step 2: Verify access checks
For functions that modify owner, config, or funds, confirm require checks or modifiers that limit callers.
Step 3: Review arithmetic
Identify multiplications and additions with user input and check whether overflow is prevented by the compiler or explicit checks.
Deliverable
Submit a short report naming each vulnerability, the exploit sequence, impact, and a prioritized recommendation.
Example findings
  • withdraw(): reentrancy via external call before state update — impact: funds drained.
  • setOwner(): missing access control — impact: attacker becomes owner and can alter state.
  • getReward(): unchecked multiplication — impact: reward overflow or inflation in older compilers.
Reflection prompt

Which of the identified issues allows immediate fund theft, and which requires further steps by the attacker?

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three critical cards to carry forward

narration.text: Keep three compact ideas in mind as you audit or author smart contracts. First, reentrancy arises when external calls are made before updating internal state; always check for external interactions and prefer updating state first. Second, arithmetic bugs such as overflow and underflow have real economic consequences in token and reward logic; verify compiler behavior or use guarded arithmetic when user inputs are part of calculations. Third, access control and transaction-order risks can lead to privilege takeover or economic front-running; ensure functions that change ownership or funds enforce explicit caller checks and consider commit-reveal or batching to reduce ordering sensitivity. These are not academic distinctions — each concept maps to concrete lines in real Solidity code. Train yourself to map code patterns to these concepts, and your reviews will become both faster and safer.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy, unchecked arithmetic, and missing access control are high-impact issues that should be prioritized during reviews.

Reentrancy
External calls before state updates create re-entry windows allowing repeated effects.
Integer wrap
Unchecked arithmetic can overflow or underflow, changing balances and totals in unexpected ways.
Access & Ordering
Missing caller checks and mempool visibility enable privilege takeover and front-running.
One-line takeaway

Map code patterns to these concepts and prioritize fixes that prevent theft and privilege escalation.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for secure contracts

narration.text: Keep a short checklist as you read contracts. First, check order of operations: are state changes made before any external call? Second, verify arithmetic and compiler guarantees for overflow and underflow, especially when user input scales values. Third, confirm access controls on every function that alters ownership, critical configuration, or funds. These simple reminders convert into practical audit steps: annotate the external call lines, mark arithmetic that multiplies user-supplied values, and flag any setter functions missing require checks. Repetition of these checks during code review reduces the chance that an obvious vulnerability slips through to production. End each review by answering: could this allow immediate theft, privilege takeover, front-running profit, or permanent denial of a function? That single question helps prioritize remediation. Order
Update state before external interactions to close reentrancy windows.
Arithmetic
Ensure overflow/underflow protections or bound user inputs in calculations.
Access
Require caller checks or use role-based access control for sensitive functions.
Final thought

A methodical checklist reduces the chance of missing high-impact vulnerabilities during review.
